title: NASA-ISRO NISAR Satellite Opens Radar Data to Public as Mission Nears First Anniversary
excerpt: Both L-band and S-band radar data from the $1.5 billion joint satellite are now freely available, enabling research in agriculture, disaster management, and climate science.
body:
• ISRO has released S-band SAR datasets from NISAR via its Bhoonidhi portal, with regular data available from July 8, 2026 onward.
  • NASA began continuous release of calibrated L-band data on July 20, covering all measurements collected since June 17.
  • The satellite produces dozens of terabytes daily, mapping nearly all land and ice surfaces on Earth twice every 12 days.
  • A striking radar image of an Antarctic nunatak revealed a "hummingbird" shape hidden beneath ice and snow, showcasing NISAR's subsurface imaging capabilities.

The world's most expensive Earth-imaging satellite is now delivering its data to the public. As the joint NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission approaches its first anniversary, both American and Indian science teams have opened access to the satellite's dual-frequency radar datasets — a milestone for the global earth observation community.

Dual Data Streams Go Live

ISRO's team at the Space Applications Centre in Ahmedabad began releasing S-band SAR datasets through the NRSC Bhoonidhi portal, with regular data products available from July 8, 2026 onward, according to ISRO. The S-band radar, built by ISRO, operates at a 9.4-centimeter wavelength and is particularly effective at observing vegetation canopies and surface features.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DbBoPpSGZTg/

On the American side, NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory started releasing calibrated L-band products on July 20 on a continuous basis, covering all measurements collected since June 17. The L-band instrument operates at a 24-centimeter wavelength and can penetrate tree canopies to image the ground beneath. Earlier limited releases in January and February 2026 had provided researchers with sample and pre-calibration products.

Users can access L-band data through the Alaska Satellite Facility Distributed Active Archive Center in Fairbanks, while S-band data is available through ISRO's Bhoonidhi portal.

The Antarctic 'Hummingbird'

To mark the data release, NASA unveiled a radar image that captured both scientific detail and public imagination. The L-band instrument imaged glacial ice near Nunatak Zaterjavshijsja, a mountaintop in East Antarctica that protrudes through a stream of ice flowing northeast toward the ocean. The resulting image bears an uncanny resemblance to a hummingbird.

https://x.com/IndianInfoGuid/status/2081751180078952747

"First, it's a beautiful image, with rich details of features that provide insights to how the glacier is moving. Then, because radar can often see through snow and deep into the ice, NISAR can observe fundamentally different properties of Antarctic ice than can be seen in optical imagery."

— Seongsu Jeong, Signal Analysis Engineer, NASA JPL

The colors in the image represent differences in how polarized microwave signals interact with ice surfaces. Magenta areas indicate smooth ice that reflected signals back with their original horizontal polarization. Green areas — the sharp crevasse lines that form the hummingbird's wings — show where signals scattered at different angles after penetrating the ice, a phenomenon called volume scattering.

Scale and Scope

NISAR's science output is staggering. The satellite generates dozens of terabytes of data per day, scanning from near the South Pole to above the Arctic Circle. It maps nearly all land and ice surfaces on Earth twice every 12 days at resolutions of 5 to 10 meters.

Launched on July 30, 2025, from India's Satish Dhawan Space Centre aboard an ISRO GSLV rocket, NISAR is the first satellite to carry two SAR instruments at different wavelengths. Its 12-meter deployable mesh antenna — the largest radar reflector NASA has sent into space — enables both instruments to collect data simultaneously.

The $1.5 billion mission represents one of the deepest collaborations between the two space agencies. NASA provided the L-band radar, high-rate telecommunications, and GPS receivers, while ISRO contributed the satellite bus, S-band radar, launch vehicle, and launch services.

Applications Across Sectors

The datasets support a wide range of applications: agriculture and crop monitoring, soil moisture and hydrology studies, flood and disaster management, forestry and ecosystem analysis, urban mapping, and climate research. ISRO's National Remote Sensing Centre has already used early NISAR data to create soil moisture maps covering central India and the Indo-Gangetic plains at 100-meter resolution.

The satellite has also revealed that parts of Mexico City are sinking two centimeters per month during dry season due to groundwater pumping, and made detailed observations of vegetation around Mount Rainier and Mount Saint Helens in the Pacific Northwest.

What's Next

By the end of 2026, NASA expects to release all L-band data acquired during earlier science operations. The mission is designed for a five-year operational life, promising a continuous stream of radar observations that researchers, government agencies, and startups worldwide can use to monitor a changing planet. All NISAR data remains freely available, typically within one to two days of observation and within hours during emergencies like natural disasters.
nri_angle: NISAR's open data empowers Indian researchers, startups, and academic institutions worldwide to build applications in agriculture monitoring, disaster response, and environmental science using ISRO's S-band radar technology.
